audit.title: Billing (DataLink)

dimensions.name: Answer-first extractability
dimensions.analysis: Weak. The implied question "How does DataLink billing work?" is never answered; the page says only "contact us to discuss your specific requirements." No liftable answer exists.

dimensions.name: Structural scannability & chunkability
dimensions.analysis: Weak. One H1, one section, no H2/H3, no tables or lists. Nothing to chunk beyond a single sentence (measured: 1 heading, 30 words total).

dimensions.name: Concrete statistics & specifics
dimensions.analysis: Absent. Measured 0 numerals, 0 units, no prices, tiers, or limits — the single highest-lift gap for a billing page.

dimensions.name: Citations & authoritative references
dimensions.analysis: Weak. Two links (one internal `llms.txt`, one contact page); 0 primary sources. No link to a pricing spec or terms.

dimensions.name: Quotable canonical definitions
dimensions.analysis: Weak. No definition of the DataLink billing model or any billable unit.

dimensions.name: Machine-readability & metadata
dimensions.analysis: Weak. Measured: no JSON-LD, canonical MISSING, no datePublished/dateModified, no OG/Twitter tags. Head metadata could not be verified — CLI should pass raw `<head>`.

dimensions.name: Code completeness & agent-runnability
dimensions.analysis: Not applicable content, but scored 0 — no examples of a billing query, invoice payload, or usage API.

dimensions.name: Query/intent coverage
dimensions.analysis: Weak. Fails "how much does DataLink cost?", "how am I billed?", "what payment methods?", "billing cadence?" — none covered.

dimensions.name: Clarity, fluency & terminology consistency
dimensions.analysis: Adequate; the one sentence is clear. Nothing else to judge.

audit.summary: This is a near-empty stub: a single 30-word section that answers no billing question and instead defers the reader to a contact form. Its only strengths are that the one sentence is grammatical and it links to `llms.txt`. The biggest opportunity is simply to publish actual billing content — pricing model, units of charge, payment methods, billing cadence — because right now there is nothing for a generative engine to retrieve, cite, or synthesize on DataLink billing. Honest verdict: the page cannot compete for any billing query and will be skipped or hallucinated over.

recommendations.title: Publish real billing content
recommendations.issue: "contact us to discuss your specific requirements and use case."
recommendations.change: Add sections answering the actual questions: what is billed (per-request / per-data-stream / subscription), pricing units, billing cycle, accepted payment methods, and where invoices appear. Keep the contact link as a closing CTA, not the whole page.
recommendations.why: A page with zero substantive answer cannot be retrieved or cited; content is the prerequisite for every other dimension.

recommendations.title: Add concrete pricing specifics
recommendations.change: State whatever is publicly quotable — tier names, price units, minimums, free-tier limits, currency. Even "pricing is usage-based, billed monthly in USD" plus a table of billable dimensions beats an empty page.
recommendations.why: Quantitative specifics are the highest-lift change for generative visibility; a billing page with no numbers underperforms sharply.

recommendations.title: Add symptom/query-phrased headings
recommendations.issue: no headings match how users ask.
recommendations.change: Add H2s like "How is DataLink billed?", "How much does DataLink cost?", "What payment methods are supported?", "When are invoices issued?"
recommendations.why: Devs and agents query by question phrasing; question-titled sections win retrieval that concept prose loses.

recommendations.title: Add a canonical billing-model definition
recommendations.issue: no self-contained statement of the billing model.
recommendations.change: Open with one liftable sentence, e.g. "DataLink billing is [usage-based/subscription], charged per [unit] and invoiced [cadence]."
recommendations.why: A crisp first-sentence definition is what engines lift verbatim.

recommendations.title: Add page metadata
recommendations.issue: no JSON-LD, canonical MISSING, no dateModified.
recommendations.change: Add `TechArticle` JSON-LD, a canonical URL, and a visible last-updated date.
recommendations.why: Structured metadata and freshness signals raise parseability and trust (E-E-A-T). Lower priority than content — schema cannot help a page with nothing to retrieve.

recommendations.title: Link to authoritative sources
recommendations.issue: only a contact link; 0 primary sources.
recommendations.change: Link to DataLink product overview, terms of service, and any published pricing/rate page.
recommendations.why: Inline links to canonical sources raise credibility and citation rate.

antiPatterns: Content-thin stub / placeholder page: the entire body defers to "contact us," which reads as marketing deflection rather than documentation.
Undated content: no visible last-updated signal (measured: dateModified absent).
offPageNotes: `llms.txt` is referenced — good site-level signal; ensure this page is actually indexed in it with a meaningful description.
Site-level schema and canonical-URL conventions appear absent here; verify they are injected at the template level and pass raw `<head>` to the CLI for a full metadata read.

If DataLink pricing is genuinely bespoke/contract-only, publish the *structure* of billing (units, cadence, process) even if exact prices stay quote-based — otherwise engines will hallucinate pricing.
